opening.headline: KEDA's ScaledObject and trigger resolve the issue where queue buildup does not scale with CPU metrics.
body: In some cases, when inference requests accumulate in the message queue and cause long waiting times, worker pods may experience significant I/O waiting, resulting in low CPU utilization. As a result, CPU-based Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) determines that the desired target is not met and does not scale up the pods. The bottleneck exists in the queue, but the metric being monitored is only CPU.

In this lesson, we examine KEDA's architecture that monitors event sources to trigger scaling, the components of a ScaledObject, the meaning of polling intervals and cooldown periods, and the Prometheus trigger along with activation thresholds. Finally, we explore use cases and configuration adjustments where queue-based scaling is more appropriate than CPU-based scaling.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the composition and triggers of KEDA ScaledObject
You can distinguish between indicator-based scaling and event-based scaling.

screens.title: It does not expand as the queue builds up.
screens.lead: Alternate between the two states and compare what differs when viewing the same scenario through CPU metrics versus queue length.

visual.alt: There are numerous requests queued up, yet the worker pod's CPU gauge shows low utilization.
labels: Fall short of target CPU: maintain pod count

states.label: When viewing CPU metrics
states.body: Although inference requests are accumulating in the message queue, the worker pods maintain low CPU utilization because they are waiting for responses from the model server. The CPU-based Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) determines that the target is not met and therefore does not scale out the pods. As the waiting time gradually increases, the autoscaler mistakenly perceives the system as idle. This is a typical issue where the scaling metric fails to reflect the bottleneck.

states.label: By queue length
states.body: Viewing the same situation through the number of tasks queued, the bottleneck becomes clearly evident. As the queue grows longer, it sends an expansion signal; when the queue empties, it sends a scaling-down signal. Since it directly counts how many tasks are backed up, it does not go through the CPU. KEDA monitors such event sources to trigger scaling.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how the current extension metrics are being defined.

screens.title: Have you ever used queue length or request volume as a metric?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process unfolds. Please don't submit or input anything yet—first reflect on your own service, then try it.

items.prompt: Is the bottleneck of our service the CPU or the queue?
items.answer: If the structure is similar to asynchronous inference, where requests go through a queue, the bottleneck appears before the CPU, in the queue. The CPU utilization observed may merely be a late reflection of the bottleneck.

items.prompt: Is this value exposed in a location accessible to the cluster?
items.answer: Queue length or request rate should be exposed as metrics in a monitoring system to be usable for scaling. If such queries are already stored in places like Prometheus, they can be directly used as scaling signals.

items.prompt: Can we scale pods down to zero when there is no traffic?
items.answer: The basic HPA maintains at least one replica. To scale down to zero, a separate component is required that wakes up the pod when new work arrives. KEDA handles the transition between zero and one.

screens.outro: Then we will examine the configuration of ScaledObject, KEDA's core resource.

screens.title: KEDA and ScaledObject Configuration
screens.lead: When you select the diagram number marker, you can view detailed descriptions for each component.

visual.alt: A diagram showing ScaledObject defining the target workload, trigger, and replica range, and KEDA generating a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) to drive the scaling.

markers.label: Target designation
markers.title: scaleTargetRef
markers.body: Refers to the workload to be scaled. `name` is required and the default type is Deployment. The target can be a Deployment, a StatefulSet, or a custom resource containing a scale subresource. If the name is incorrect, the target will not be found and nothing will be scaled.

markers.label: Copy range
markers.title: minReplicaCount and maxReplicaCount
markers.body: The default value of `minReplicaCount` is 0, and the default value of `maxReplicaCount` is 100. If the minimum is set to 0, it will decrease down to 0 during idle states; if set to 1, exactly one pod will always remain. The maximum represents the upper limit during overload conditions.

markers.label: trigger
markers.title: triggers
markers.body: List of sources that trigger expansion. There are many scalers such as queues, streams, databases, and Prometheus. Multiple triggers can be configured together, and each trigger includes metadata such as source address and threshold value.

markers.label: HPA Generation
markers.title: The HPA developed by KEDA
markers.body: KEDA creates HPA from ScaledObject and delegates scaling from 1 to N ranges to HPA. In other words, KEDA does not replace HPA but instead provides HPA with workload-based metrics.

markers.label: Between 0 and 1
markers.title: Activation and Deactivation
markers.body: HPA does not scale to zero or recover from zero. The activation and deactivation between zero and one is handled directly by KEDA. Because of this boundary, separate settings for detection speed (polling) and idle time (cooldown) are required.

screens.outro: We will now examine the polling interval and cooldown affected at this boundary.

screens.title: Poling interval and cooldown
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the pollingInterval value. You can observe how the speed at which a service in idle state detects work changes depending on the value.

stops.body: When the pods are at zero, KEDA checks every 10 seconds to trigger. Even if work is enqueued, it takes at most about 10 seconds to wake up from 0 to 1. While detection is fast, frequent queries to the source result in increased load on the queue or Prometheus. The waiting time for the first request must be a value appropriate for the service.

This is the default value. Even if work is enqueued, it may take up to approximately 30 seconds for the system to wake up from 0 to 1. This is not an error but a symptom arising from this value. Polling from 0 to 1 is handled by KEDA, while reading metrics from 1 to N is performed by HPA according to its own periodicity.

Although the service wakes up from a suspended state with a maximum delay of about 60 seconds, it is sufficient for services that wait for their first task as in nightly scheduling. However, this delay is significant when users are waiting for a response.

Cool down is a separate setting. `cooldownPeriod: 300` is the duration to wait before reducing the value to zero, starting from the last time the pod was active. It is not an error that a pod remains for five minutes even when the queue is empty—it is due to this value. Cool down applies only when reduced to zero; reductions from 1 to N are handled by the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA).

`fallback` is a safety mechanism that restores the replica count to a predefined value when a scaler experiences consecutive failures. For example, if `failureThreshold: 3` and `replicas: 6` are configured, after three consecutive failures, the replica count is reduced to six. This prevents the service from dropping to zero and halting operation when metrics are unavailable. Reducing the polling interval improves detection speed, but also remember that it increases the load on the source and the number of queries exchanged.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the actual trigger configuration for the Prometheus trigger.

screens.title: Prometheus Triggers and Activation Thresholds
screens.lead: In the trigger settings below, select each highlighted section one at a time to verify the role of each field and the symptoms that occur when it is used incorrectly.

data.text:
triggers:
- type: prometheus
  metadata:
    serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
    query: sum(inference_queue_depth)
    threshold: "20"
    activationThreshold: "0"

marks.note: This is the Prometheus server address to which the query will be sent. It is a required field; if incorrect, the metrics will not be readable. In this case, if the previously mentioned `fallback` is missing, the extension may halt or remain in an unintended state.

The PromQL to execute. The result must be a single value. If multiple values are returned, resembling pod-level time series, it would violate the requirement, so aggregation functions such as `sum` are used to consolidate them into a single value. For example, if request rate is used, `sum(rate(http_requests_total[2m]))` would be an appropriate form.

This is the target value when starting expansion. It can be understood as the queue length that a single pod can handle. Based on this value, the HPA calculates the target replica count within the range from 1 to N.

The default baseline for the 0-to-1 transition is 0. The state becomes active only when the value exceeds this baseline. It is important to note that the activation threshold and the expansion target value serve different purposes. The activation threshold serves as the baseline for the 0↔1 transition, while the threshold serves as the baseline for the 1-to-N range.

Types of triggers. In addition, `namespace` and `customHeaders` are used to handle environments like Thanos or authentication headers, and `ignoreNullValues` defaults to true, which ignores empty results; setting it to false causes an error when the target disappears.

screens.title: Explanation: Queue length-based expansion is more suitable than CPU-based expansion, and how to adjust the settings
screens.lead: The instructor provides a step-by-step explanation of the process of reading and modifying the extension settings of asynchronous inference workers. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: The queue length determines the number of pods, and the queue decreases down to zero when it is empty.
labels: Job arrives in queue: detected by polling, from 0 to 1
Queue growth: HPA scales from 1 to N
When queue is high, cool down and set to 0.

steps.title: situation
steps.body:
This is a worker service where asynchronous inference requests accumulate in a queue. Since CPU utilization is low, no scaling is performed based on CPU usage; instead, the queue grows longer. The team upgraded to KEDA and implemented the following configuration.

```
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: infer-worker
  minReplicaCount: 1
  triggers:
  - type: prometheus
    metadata:
      serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
      query: inference_queue_depth
      threshold: "20"
```

steps.title: Step 1: Read the minimum replication count
steps.body: Because it is set to `minReplicaCount: 1`, a pod remains active even when the queue is empty. For services with long idle periods, such as overnight operations, this remaining pod incurs idle costs. To reduce the value to zero, set it to 0 (the default value). Remember that even if the cooldown period has passed, if the minimum value is set to 1, one pod will still remain active.

steps.title: Step 2: Read the query
steps.body: If `inference_queue_depth` returns multiple values in a pod-wise time series, it violates the requirement that a single value must be returned. Instead, use an aggregation like `sum(inference_queue_depth)` to combine them into one. This way, the queue length for the entire service is conveyed as a single number.

steps.title: Step 3: Set the threshold value
steps.body: `threshold` is set to the queue length that a single pod can handle. If set to 20, when the queue reaches 60, the target number of pods will approach 3. `activationThreshold` is set to a value greater than 0 (default 0), so that when work items appear in the queue, it increments from 0 to 1. The activation threshold and the target expansion value are specified separately.

steps.title: Step 4: Verify idle processing
steps.body: When queue length is high, the cooldown (default 300 seconds) decreases to zero, and polling (default 30 seconds) detects and raises requests. The first request can wait up to approximately 30 seconds, plus the time required for the pod to become ready. If this delay is not acceptable, reduce `pollingInterval` or set the minimum to 1. Either option represents a trade-off between cost and delay.

steps.title: Step 5: Distinguish between the two methods
steps.body: Indicator-based scaling, such as CPU or memory ratio, scales based on the results of work processed. Event-based scaling directly measures the workload that needs to be processed. A bottleneck service with work queued has a faster response time with the latter approach.

steps.title: result
steps.body: Extended to reflect bottlenecks, reducing waiting times and dropping to zero during idle periods, thereby lowering costs. The configuration required precisely reading one minimum replica, one query, and two thresholds.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Extends indicators to reflect bottlenecks
screens.lead: This course covers the structure and configuration of KEDA, summarized into a single flow.

paragraphs: ScaledObject declares the target to scale, the range of replicas, and the trigger that initiates scaling. KEDA uses this to generate a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) responsible for managing the scale from 1 to N, while directly handling activation between 0 and 1. KEDA is not a replacement for HPA but rather a component that provides event-based signals to the HPA.

The polling interval sets the speed at which the system detects workloads in idle state, and the cooldown defines the waiting time before reducing it to zero. The activation threshold is based on increasing from 0 to 1, while the expansion threshold aims for a target value from 1 to N. Queries from Prometheus triggers must return a single value.

Indicator-based scaling follows the results of processing, while event-based scaling follows the workloads that need to be processed. If a bottleneck exists in a queue, even with low CPU utilization, work accumulates, making a direct indicator of workload more appropriate.

Going back to the initial scene, the reason the system did not scale despite queue buildup was that the indicator did not detect a bottleneck. Aligning scaling signals with the actual bottleneck is both the starting point and the conclusion of this lesson. After configuring the settings, monitor both queue length and pod count together to fine-tune the thresholds.

callout.label: organizing
callout.text: Expand to include indicators that reflect bottlenecks.

glossary.def: This is a custom resource defined by KEDA to scale target workloads based on triggers.
This defines the source that retrieves extended signals such as queue, stream, and indicator.
KEDA's trigger verification period, with a default value of 30 seconds.
This is the time elapsed from when activity was active until it is reduced to zero, with a default value of 300 seconds.
A trigger that expands Prometheus query results by comparing against thresholds.

misconceptions.fact: KEDA creates HPA from ScaledObject to handle the 1-to-N range, and only directly manages the transition between 0 and 1.

misconceptions.myth: cooldownPeriod is applied to all reductions.
misconceptions.fact: Cool-down applies only when set to 0. Shrinking within the 1 to N range is handled by HPA.

misconceptions.myth: Low CPU utilization indicates that the service is idle.
misconceptions.fact: If the bottleneck exists in the queue, the system accumulates waiting even if the CPU utilization is low. Utilization reflects the result of the bottleneck but may not directly indicate the presence of the bottleneck itself.

misconceptions.myth: Even when minReplicaCount is set to 1, the queue count can drop down to 0 when the queue is empty.
misconceptions.fact: If the minimum replica count is set to 1, one pod remains even after the cooldown period ends. To reduce it to 0, set the minimum replica count to 0.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Expand to include indicators that reflect bottlenecks.
ScaledObject declares the target, trigger, and replica range, and KEDA creates an HPA.
The polling interval sets the detection speed, while cooldown establishes the state prior to setting it to zero.
The activation threshold ranges from 0 to 1, while the expansion threshold ranges from 1 to N.
